The appellant, who was the sole executor of the will, claimed a declaration that the said Lakshmamma was the owner of the properties mentioned in the schedule attached to the plaint and as such was entitled to dispose of them by a will. The appellant claimed a decree for possession against respondent 1 in respect of items 3, 4 and 5 and a declaration that respondent I was entitled to deal with them by a Will. The appellant also claimed a declaration in respect of the properties which were the subject matter of the will. The respondent 1 claimed a declaration of the will and claimed to be the owner of properties which were his properties. The appellant 's case was that the will was executed by one G and was not a will and that the will had been revoked by the will. It was further alleged that the will itself was revoked by the appellant and that the appellant had executed a will in favour of the respondent. The appellant contended that the will executed by G was not a Will and that the respondent had no power to revoke the will. Held, that the will did not create a will in the will and that it was not a testamentary disposition. The will was not a document of title and was not compulsorily registrable. The will had been executed by G in his capacity as the sole executor and not as a will. It could not be revoked by the respondent. It was not a disposition of the property and was not capable of being revoked by the testator. The will did not confer any right on the respondent. There was no question of the respondent being revoked by him. The will could not be revoke by the appellant. The will itself was not a valid document. The will in the present case was not a deed of gift. The will, therefore, did not create any interest in the properties. The will created a will in respect of all the properties covered by the will and the appellant was not entitled to revoke it. The will executed by the respondent in his capacity of the appellant was a will and not a will.

The appellant was charged with the offence of murder. The prosecution case was that the appellant caused the death of Sheo Sahai and that he was falsely implicated in the case. The appellant denied the allegation that he had caused the death. The trial court acquitted him but the High Court acquitted him. The appellant contended that the entire report was inadmissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a confession of the offence by the appellant made to a Police Officer and that the evidence relied on by the High Court was insufficient to establish that the appellant had murdered Sheo Sahai. Held, that the entire prosecution case was not proved beyond reasonable doubt and the appellant was rightly convicted. The extra judicial confession of the appellant to the Police Officer was admissible in evidence and the evidence relied upon by the High court was insufficient to prove that the appellant committed the murder of Sheo Sahai. The extrajudicial confession of the accused to the Police officer was inadmissible in the evidence as its disclosure to the Police was not proved. The extra Judicial confession of the co accused to the police officer was inadmissible under section 27 of the Evidence Act. The extra-judicial confession of a co accused to a Police officer was admissible in the evidence and the conviction of the appellant was not illegal. The extra evidence of the appellant in the present case was inadmissible in view of the fact that the appellant was falsely implicated. The extra examination of the appellant by the Police Officer did not affect his case. The extra investigation of the case was not made in accordance with the provisions of the Evidence. The extra enquiry was not made by the Police officer in accordance with section 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The evidence of the prosecution witnesses was not sufficient to prove the extra judicial confession. The extra police investigation was not made according to the provisions of section 162 of Code of Criminal procedure. The evidence was not admissible in evidence as it was not corroborated by any direct evidence. The extra criminal investigation was not an essential part of the prosecution case. The evidence relied on was not sufficient for establishing the guilt of the appellant. The extra illegal investigation was not a substantive piece of evidence and the appellant could not be convicted on the basis of the extra judicial confessions. The extra 'judicial confession of an accused was inadmissible in a trial for the offence of conspiracy under section 120B I.P.C. The appellant was rightly acquitted.

The question for decision was whether sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was necessary for prosecuting the appellant under section 409, and whether sanction under that section was necessary. Held, that the prosecution which had resulted in the conviction of the appellant was not competent. The sanction under section197(1) was necessary only when the acts complained of were committed by a public servant in the discharge of his official duties. The sanction was necessary when the acts were committed by the public servant in discharge of his duty as a public servant. The sanction must be in respect of acts done by the public servants in discharge of their official duties. It is not necessary that the acts complained or the official character of the public servant should be such as to amount to an offence. The sanction is necessary when the act complained of is done by a public officer in the discharge or purported discharge of his duties as a public officer. The sanction may be necessary when the public servant is in the discharge, or purported discharge, of his duties, as a public official. The sanction need not be in respect to acts done by a person in the discharge o the discharge of the duties as a private individual. The sanction should be in respect only of acts done in the discharge and purported discharge of the duty as a private person. The sanction can be only in respect of the acts done by him in the discharge. The sanction could be only in relation to acts done in discharge of the official duties as a pubic individual. The appellant was detained under the , under the , on the ground that he was an Advocate of the High Court of Bombay. The grounds of detention were served on him along with the order of detention. The grounds were served on the appellant along with the grounds of detention. On the same day, the appellant was served with the grounds and the grounds of his detention were served upon him. The grounds and the material were supplied to him. The appellant was served the grounds of the detention and the grounds were served upon the appellant. The grounds served on the detenu were the same as the grounds served on him. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant contended that the grounds of order of detention were vague and that the grounds were vague. Held, that the grounds served upon the detenu were vague and the grounds served were vague. The order of detention was not vitiated by the non disclosure of the grounds of their detention. The order was not vitiated on the ground of non disclosure of grounds of detention and the order was not bad on the ground specified in section 3(5) of the . The grounds served were not vague. The grounds supplied to the detenu were not vague and the order of the detention was not bad. The order did not disclose the grounds of action and the grounds did not disclose any particulars of the grounds. The order could not be said to be mala fide. The order had to be communicated to the detenue at the time when the grounds were furnished. The order not to disclose particulars of the facts considered prejudicial to the public interest could not be held to have hampered his constitutional right of representation and an obligation to communicate cannot be implied in these circumstances. The necessity for such a communication would arise only if the detenue, feeling the grounds to be vague, ask for particulars. An obligation to communicate the decision not to disclose facts considered prejudicial t the public interest may well be implied in such a situation. But in the absence of any such request by the detenue, the non communication of the decision cannot be held to be mala fides. The necessity of such a communication must arise only if there is a reasonable cause for the detention of the person concerned.

The appellants were the trustees of a temple in the State of Madras. The properties were granted in Inam to the ancestor of the appellants. The appellants claimed that the properties were granted to the ancestor, and that the properties belonged to the temple. The appellants pleaded that the properties had been granted to the predecessor of the appellants, and that they had established their title to the properties. The trial Judge held that the appellants had proved their title to them and that the appellants were entitled to the possession of the properties. On appeal, the High Court held that the alienor must be deemed to have resigned his office or left it. The appellants came to this Court by special leave. The appellants contended that the properties in suit had not been granted to them by the respondent No. 4, and that their case was that the properties did not belong to the temple and were not the properties of the temple. HELD : (i) The appellants had proved the title of the appellants to the properties and the High Court was right in holding that the alienors had proved their possession. The appellants had failed to establish their title to their properties. [123 F] (ii) The appellants were entitled only to the properties which were granted to them. The appellants were not holding the properties as managers of the temple, and the question whether the alienor had been removed from the management of the temple did not arise. [123 G] (iii) The appellants could not be held to have acquired title to the property by prescription. The appellants could have proved their title by adverse possession. [123 H] (iv) The appellants ' case that the alienees had been removed by the respondent Nos. 4, 5 and 6 was not correct. The appellants ' claim that the alienee had been removed was not correct, because the alienees were not holding any temple as managers of a temple. The alienees had not been removed from management of the trust. [124 H] (v) The appellants must be deemed not to have been removed from their management. [125 A] (vi) The appellants cannot be held to be entitled to the properties in question. [126 B] (vii) The appellants have proved their possession of the property in suit. [126 C]

The appellants were convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and each was sentenced to death. The appellants appealed to the High Court and their petition was dismissed. The appellants contended that the conviction was illegal and that the sentence of death was not warranted by the evidence. Held, that the conviction of the appellants under section 302 was not justified. The conviction of the appellant under section 302 could not be sustained because the evidence showed that the appellants were not guilty of the offence of murder. The conviction under section 302, therefore, was not justified and the conviction was not justified on the evidence. The conviction was not warranted on the evidence and the conviction could not be justified on the ground that the evidence was not sufficient to justify the conviction. The conviction could not therefore be sustained on the evidence, because the evidence was of a circumstantial nature and the circumstances of the case were such that it could not be said that the appellants had committed the murder.

The appellant, who was the owner of a piece of land, granted a lease for a period of 20 years to the respondent, who was a minor, for a period not exceeding one year. The respondent 's lease was renewed for a period exceeding one year, and the appellant was required to pay the lease amount within two months. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court, challenging the validity of the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act, and the order of the Government, directing the Government to hold an enquiry under section 20(2) of the Act, and to pass an order of termination of the lease. The High Court dismissed the writ petition, but granted a certificate under article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution. Held, that the second proviso was not intended to be a complete code in itself, and the second proviso did not make the right created after July 1, 1945, a new right in the appellant, and the Government must do something to avoid them. The second proviso was enacted to nullify the creation of rights in anticipation of the legislation and hence it was not intended that the Government must have the right to terminate the lease.
